summary: A lead screw is an inclined plane wrapped around a shaft. You derive the torque, the efficiency and the self-locking condition from the force balance on a thread, compare a sliding Acme screw with a ball screw, and check the closed-form efficiency against a direct force-balance solution.
html:
The thread as a ramp

Unroll one turn of a thread with mean diameter dm​ and lead l (axial travel per turn). It becomes a ramp of length πdm​ rising l, at the lead angle

tanλ=πdm​l​.

Pushing an axial load F up that ramp with a tangential force P, against friction μ with friction angle φ=arctanμ, the force balance gives

P=Ftan(λ+φ),Traise​=P2dm​​=2Fdm​​tan(λ+φ).

Without friction the torque would be Fl/(2π), by energy conservation, so the efficiency is

η=2πTraise​Fl​=tan(λ+φ)tanλ​.

For an Acme or trapezoidal thread, the flank angle (half-angle α, 14.5° for Acme, 15° for metric trapezoidal) tilts the normal force, so use μ′=μ/cosα.

Back-driving

Can the load turn the screw on its own? Lowering needs torque Tlower​=2Fdm​​tan(φ−λ). If that’s positive (φ>λ), you must turn the screw to lower the load: it’s self-locking, which is convenient for a jack or a Z axis that must hold position with the power off. If λ>φ the load back-drives the screw with efficiency

η′=tanλtan(λ−φ)​.

A self-locking screw has η<50 % (with φ>λ, tanλ/tan(λ+φ)<tanλ/tan2λ<1/2). You can’t have both a high-efficiency drive and a power-off brake from friction alone.

Ball screws replace sliding with rolling balls, μ≈0.003–0.01, giving 90 % or more efficiency in both directions. They always back-drive, so a vertical axis needs a brake.

Worked example

Push 500 N with a 12 mm screw.

  1. Trapezoidal, 2 mm lead, μ=0.15: λ=arctan(2/(π⋅12))=3.04°, φ=8.53°, so η=0.0531/0.2048=25.9 %. Torque =500⋅0.002/(2π⋅0.259)=0.614 N·m. It’s self-locking.
  2. Ball screw, 5 mm lead, μ=0.005: λ=7.55°, φ=0.29°, η=96.3 %, torque 0.413 N·m. It back-drives with η′=96.1 %.
  3. Motor speed for 50 mm/s: 25 rev/s with the 2 mm screw, 10 rev/s with the 5 mm one.

Code it from scratch

lead_screw.py
import numpy as np

def efficiency(lead, dm, mu):
    lam, phi = np.arctan(lead / (np.pi * dm)), np.arctan(mu)
    return np.tan(lam) / np.tan(lam + phi)

def back_efficiency(lead, dm, mu):
    lam, phi = np.arctan(lead / (np.pi * dm)), np.arctan(mu)
    return np.tan(lam - phi) / np.tan(lam) if lam > phi else 0.0

def push_force_balance(F, lam, mu):
    """Block on a ramp of angle lam, pushed horizontally by P, sliding up against friction.
    Unknowns [P, N]: sum of forces along the ramp and normal to it."""
    A = np.array([[np.cos(lam), -mu],               # P cos - F sin - mu N = 0
                  [-np.sin(lam), 1.0]])             # N - F cos - P sin = 0
    rhs = np.array([F * np.sin(lam), F * np.cos(lam)])
    P, N = np.linalg.solve(A, rhs)
    return P

def raise_torque(F, lead, dm, mu):
    lam = np.arctan(lead / (np.pi * dm))
    return push_force_balance(F, lam, mu) * dm / 2

if __name__ == "__main__":
    for lead, dm, mu in [(0.002, 0.012, 0.15), (0.005, 0.012, 0.005), (0.010, 0.020, 0.1), (0.04, 0.012, 0.2)]:
        T = raise_torque(500, lead, dm, mu)
        eta_energy = 500 * lead / (2 * np.pi * T)            # work out / work in over one turn
        print(f"lead {lead*1e3:.0f} mm, d {dm*1e3:.0f} mm, mu {mu}: T = {T:.3f} N*m, "
              f"eta {eta_energy:.4f} (formula {efficiency(lead, dm, mu):.4f}), back {back_efficiency(lead, dm, mu):.3f}")
        assert abs(eta_energy - efficiency(lead, dm, mu)) < 1e-12
    assert back_efficiency(0.002, 0.012, 0.15) == 0.0                     # self-locking
    assert efficiency(0.002, 0.012, 0.15) < 0.5
    assert back_efficiency(0.005, 0.012, 0.005) > 0.95                    # a ball screw back-drives
    # every self-locking geometry is below 50 % efficient
    lam = np.radians(np.linspace(0.1, 44, 400))
    for mu in (0.05, 0.1, 0.2):
        phi = np.arctan(mu); locking = lam < phi
        assert np.all(np.tan(lam[locking]) / np.tan(lam[locking] + phi) < 0.5)

Exercises

A 3D printer’s Z axis uses an 8 mm screw with 8 mm lead (μ = 0.2, brass nut). Does the bed fall when the motor is switched off?

Show the solution

λ=arctan(8/(π⋅8))=17.7° and φ=11.3°. Since λ>φ it back-drives, so the bed can drift down under its weight (often the stepper’s detent torque holds it). A 2 mm-lead screw (λ=4.5°) would self-lock.

Why does the Acme flank angle increase the effective friction?

Show the solution

The thread flank is tilted by α, so the normal force needed to carry the axial load F is F/cosα, larger than F. Friction is μ times that normal force, so the effective coefficient is μ/cosα, about 3 % more for 14.5°.

Efficiency in % of that screw with μ = 0.15?
Torque in N·m to push 500 N with it?
Efficiency in % of a 5 mm lead ball screw (12 mm, μ = 0.005)?

quiz.explain: A power-off brake from friction costs efficiency.
